opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a bit early, honestly. There's been incredible progress in the last couple of years, especially on locomotion. Walking, running, getting back up after a fall, even some pretty acrobatic stuff now works quite reliably, largely thanks to reinforcement learning in simulation and sim-to-real transfer. That part I'm fairly confident about, since it's what I've worked on for a long time.

But putting a robot in someone's home is a very different problem. The home is the most unstructured environment you can imagine. Every house is different, there are kids and pets, things are cluttered, objects get moved all the time. What you really need there is general, robust manipulation, and that's still far from solved. We can show nice demos of folding laundry or loading a dishwasher, but going from a demo that works some of the time to something that works reliably, day after day, without supervision, is a huge gap.

Then there's safety. A humanoid is a fairly heavy machine with powerful actuators. In a factory you can have safety zones and procedures. In a living room with a toddler around, the bar is much higher, and I don't think we have good answers yet for certification or for guaranteeing safe behavior from learned policies.

So when companies say they'll sell humanoids into homes next year, I read it as one of two things. Either it's a very limited product, maybe partly teleoperated or doing a narrow set of tasks, or it's an early-adopter program where people are basically paying to help collect data. That's not necessarily bad. Data is the big bottleneck, and getting robots into real environments is one way to collect it. But I'd be careful about expecting a general-purpose household helper you can just leave alone.

My feeling is that industrial and logistics settings come first, where tasks are more repetitive and the environment can be controlled a bit. Homes will come, but it's more of a several-years story than a next-year story.

r001.rationale: The response says announced home sales may be an “early-adopter program” where buyers help collect data, which clearly frames them as early-adopter trials.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm fairly skeptical about the near-term timelines. I come at this from the locomotion side, where we've spent years getting legged robots to walk robustly, and even that, which is arguably the most mature part of the stack, is not fully solved for unstructured environments. A home is about the hardest environment you could pick. It's cluttered, it changes every day, there are kids and pets and stairs and wet floors, and the robot has to be safe around people who didn't sign a waiver.

So when I hear companies say they'll be shipping into homes in the next year, I separate two things. One is the demo, which I believe. You can absolutely build a humanoid today that walks around a house, picks up a cup, and loads a dishwasher in a controlled setting. Learning-based control, sim-to-real, large-scale reinforcement learning, all of that has made huge progress, and I'm genuinely excited about it. The other is a product that works reliably for a thousand hours in a home the developers have never seen, without a teleoperator in the loop and without breaking anything. I don't think we're there, and I don't think we're a year away.

The gap is mostly in manipulation and in long-horizon autonomy, not in walking. Dexterous manipulation of arbitrary objects is still very much a research problem. We don't have the data, the hardware is fragile and expensive, and generalization to new objects and tasks is far weaker than what people see in curated videos. Then there's the question of what happens when the robot fails, because it will fail, and in a home a failure can mean a fall onto a child or a broken appliance.

That said, I don't think the ambition is wrong, and the pressure from companies is actually pushing the research forward. Early units will probably look more like a pilot program, with heavy remote supervision, limited task sets, and a lot of data collection going back to the company. I think that's fine as long as they're honest about it. What I'd push back on is the framing that this is a general-purpose home robot you can buy and forget about. I'd expect a few years of iteration in factories and warehouses first, where the environment is structured and the economics are clearer, before the home version is really ready.

r001.rationale: The response characterizes the first home units as a pilot program with remote supervision and limited tasks, equivalent to early-adopter trials.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical of that timeline. There’s a big difference between showing a robot doing a task in a demonstration and having it reliably do that task in someone’s home. Homes are very unstructured: you have different furniture, clutter, pets, children, and situations you didn’t anticipate. And the robot needs to handle those situations safely, without an engineer standing next to it.

So I can imagine companies putting robots into a small number of homes as early trials, perhaps with substantial remote assistance. But that’s quite different from selling a product that you can leave alone and expect to do useful work every day. I’d want to understand how autonomous it actually is, how often someone needs to intervene, and what happens when it fails. Those are much more meaningful measures than whether a company starts shipping next year.

r001.rationale: The response describes companies placing robots in a small number of homes as early trials, matching the criterion’s interpretation of the coming-year plans as early-adopter trials.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be skeptical of that timeline, especially if we mean a robot that can come into your home and reliably do a wide range of useful tasks. There’s a big gap between showing a compelling demo and having a system that works every day in an environment you don’t control.

In a home, you have unfamiliar objects, clutter, stairs, pets, and people moving around. The robot needs to handle all of that safely, and when something goes wrong, you can’t assume there’s an engineer standing next to it. Locomotion is only one part of the problem. Manipulation, reliability, and recovering from mistakes are all very challenging.

I can imagine limited deployments where a robot performs a few specific tasks with substantial support. But I’d distinguish that from a general-purpose household robot. I’d want to know what it can actually do, how often a person has to intervene, and how much useful work it gets done.

r001.rationale: The response allows for limited, supported deployments of specific tasks, but it does not characterize the announced home sales as early-adopter trials.
